Module 1

Booting: from the BIOS to the first user program

When a PC is switched on, no operating system is in memory. Firmware reads one 512-byte sector from a disk, jumps into it, and from that moment the operating system has to pull itself up by its own bootstraps: find more code, load it, set up the machine, and finally start a program that a user can talk to. This module follows that path in two real code bases. On MS-DOS 4.00 we read the FDISK master boot record, the FAT boot sector MSBOOT.ASM, the IO.SYS loader, and the SYSINIT module that processes CONFIG.SYS and starts COMMAND.COM. On FreeBSD 15.1 we read mbr.S and the boot0 boot manager, boot1/boot2, the BTX mini-kernel, the Lua-scripted loader, and the kernel's own start-up path from locore.S through hammer_time() and mi_startup() to start_init(), which runs /sbin/init. The module ends at exactly that point: the first user program. System calls, process creation, file systems and the shell are covered in Modules 2 and 3.

Francesco Valerio Buccoli · francesco@buccoli.com

Learning goals. After this module you can:

  • Explain the PC BIOS boot contract (load address 0000:7C00, the 0x55AA signature, the boot drive in DL, INT 13h disk services) and compute real-mode segment:offset addresses.
  • Read and annotate the MS-DOS 4.00 and FreeBSD 15.1 master boot records: relocation, the partition-table walk, the active flag, and loading the next sector.
  • Decode a FAT boot sector and its BIOS Parameter Block (BPB) field by field, and trace how MSBOOT finds and loads IO.SYS.
  • Describe FreeBSD's BIOS boot chain (boot0 or mbr, boot1, boot2 or gptboot, BTX, loader) and explain why it switches to protected mode while MS-DOS never does.
  • Trace MS-DOS initialisation from IO.SYS through SYSINIT, CONFIG.SYS and the EXEC of COMMAND.COM.
  • Trace FreeBSD kernel start-up from the loader's trampoline through btext, hammer_time() and mi_startup() to start_init().
  • Contrast MS-DOS's SYSINIT module with FreeBSD's SYSINIT() linker-set framework, including how each lets third-party code join the boot.
  • Evaluate boot-time design trade-offs (512-byte limits, writing to disk during boot, real mode versus protected mode) in the context of the hardware each system targeted.

Prerequisites.

  • C, and a first exposure to x86 assembly (registers, mov, call, int). This module teaches the 16-bit real-mode details it needs.
  • The lab environment from Module 0 (00-lab.md): QEMU, DOSBox-X, the MS-DOS 4.00 floppy image build/images/dos400.img built from this source tree, the boot blocks in build/freebsd/boot/, and the FreeBSD 15.1 amd64 VM with /usr/src.

1.1 The PC BIOS boot contract#

Real mode and segment:offset addresses#

Every x86 processor, including a modern 64-bit one, starts in real mode, the execution mode of the original 8086/8088. In real mode there is no memory protection and no paging. Addresses are formed from two 16-bit values, a segment and an offset:

linear address = segment * 16 + offset

The result is a 20-bit linear address, so real mode can reach 1 MB (0x00000-0xFFFFF). We write segment:offset pairs as 0000:7C00 and linear addresses as 0x7C00. Many pairs name the same byte: 0000:7C00, 07C0:0000 and 0700:0C00 all denote linear 0x7C00. The segment registers are CS (code), DS and ES (data) and SS (stack); lodsb implicitly reads DS:SI and stosb writes ES:DI. A far jump (JMP FAR, opcode 0xEA) loads both CS and IP; a near jump only changes IP. Most boot code sets DS, ES and SS to zero so that offsets equal linear addresses in the first 64 KB.

A paragraph is 16 bytes, the granularity of segments. MS-DOS sizes almost everything in paragraphs; you will see shifts by 4 (* 16) and by 6 (KB to paragraphs: * 1024 / 16) throughout its start-up code.

What the BIOS does#

The BIOS (Basic Input/Output System) is firmware in ROM. After its power-on self test it reads the first sector of the boot device (cylinder 0, head 0, sector 1) to linear address 0x7C00, on most machines checks that the last two bytes are 0x55, 0xAA, and jumps to it in real mode with the BIOS drive number in DL (0x00 for the first floppy, 0x80 for the first hard disk). Both code bases describe this contract in their own comments.

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 1.1 – MSBOOT's own description of what the ROM does before it runs (MSBOOT.ASM lines 30-39)Source ↗
; The ROM in the IBM PC starts the boot process by performing a hardware
; initialization and a verification of all external devices.  If all goes
; well, it will then load from the boot drive the sector from track 0, head 0,
; sector 1.  This sector is placed at physical address 07C00h.  The initial
; registers are set up as follows:  CS=DS=ES=SS=0.  IP=7C00h, SP=0400H.
;
; The code in this sector is responsible for locating the MSDOS device drivers
; (IBMBIO) and for placing the directory sector with this information at
; physical address 00500h.  After loading in this sector, it reads in the
; entirety of the BIOS at BIOSEG:0 and does a long jump to that point.

The comment records the IBM PC's behaviour in the mid-1980s (SP=0400H, all segment registers zero). Later BIOSes do not guarantee those values, and neither system relies on them: both reload DS, ES, SS and SP first. Neither reloads CS: both rely on the BIOS entering at CS:IP = 0:7C00. FreeBSD's boot0 documents the weaker modern contract: only CS:IP = 0:0x7c00 and the drive number in DL (boot0.S lines 78-89).

Two parts of the contract matter in what follows. First, the signature: a boot sector ends with the bytes 0x55, 0xAA. MS-DOS writes them as db 55h,0aah; FreeBSD writes the little-endian word .word 0xaa55 (MAGIC), which is the same two bytes. Second, the boot drive: the BIOS passes it in DL, but, as we will see, MS-DOS's boot sector ignores DL for its reads and uses a drive number that FORMAT stored inside the sector.

The BIOS services the boot code uses#

Boot code cannot contain disk or screen drivers; it calls the BIOS through software interrupts. The interrupt vector table (IVT) at linear 0x0000-0x03FF holds 256 four-byte segment:offset pointers, and INT n calls the routine at vector n. The BIOS data area (BDA) at 0x0400-0x04FF holds firmware variables. The table lists the main ones our two systems use; boot0 also reads the 18.2 Hz tick counter (INT 1Ah) for its timeout, and boot1 asks for the drive geometry (INT 13h AH=08h).

Service Purpose MS-DOS 4.00 example FreeBSD 15.1 example
INT 13h AH=02h Read sectors by cylinder/head/sector (CHS) DOCALL in MSBOOT main.7 in mbr.S
INT 13h AH=03h Write sectors not used by any boot sector boot0 write-back
INT 13h AH=00h Reset the disk system MSBOOT line 201 boot1 retry
INT 13h AH=41h/42h EDD ("packet", LBA) read not used mbr.S main.5
INT 10h AH=0Eh Print one character (teletype) WRITE putstr
INT 16h Read or poll the keyboard wait for a key boot0 read_key
INT 12h Conventional memory size in KB MSLOAD BTX reads the same value from BDA 0x413 (BDA_MEM)
INT 18h "No bootable device" FDBOOT line 45 mbr.S line 70
INT 19h Re-run the bootstrap MSBOOT line 282 boot1 jumps to F000:FFF0 instead (lines 242-243)

CHS addressing names a sector by cylinder (0-1023), head (0-255) and sector (1-63). INT 13h packs these into registers in a way that only makes sense historically: CH holds the low 8 bits of the cylinder, bits 6-7 of CL hold cylinder bits 8-9, bits 0-5 of CL hold the sector, and DH holds the head. The partition-table entries of an MBR use the same packed format (boot0.S lines 65-73), which is why both MBRs can load CX and DH straight from a table entry. The 10-bit cylinder field limits CHS to 1024 cylinders; boot1 checks exactly this (cmpl $0x3ff,%eax, boot1.S lines 311-313). The Enhanced Disk Drive (EDD) extensions remove the limit: INT 13h AH=42h takes a 16-byte disk address packet holding a 64-bit logical block address (LBA). MS-DOS 4.00 predates these extensions; FreeBSD uses them whenever the BIOS reports support.

Memory in the first megabyte#

The diagram shows the first megabyte as the boot code of both systems uses it. Addresses are linear.

The FreeBSD addresses come from the .set lines in boot1.S and btx.S; the MS-DOS ones from MSBOOT.ASM's EQUs. The upper limit of conventional memory is not a constant: both systems ask the BIOS. On a 640 KB machine it is 0xA0000.

UEFI is out of scope#

Modern PCs usually boot through UEFI firmware, which loads PE/COFF executables from a FAT-formatted EFI system partition and never runs a 512-byte boot sector. FreeBSD 15.1 supports UEFI with a separate loader under stand/efi, which this module does not cover. Everything below assumes a BIOS boot, which is also what QEMU's default firmware (SeaBIOS) provides in the lab.

1.2 The master boot record#

A hard disk can hold several operating systems, so its first sector does not belong to any one of them. That sector, the master boot record (MBR), contains a small program, a 64-byte partition table at offset 0x1BE with four 16-byte entries, and the signature at 0x1FE. Each entry describes one partition (FreeBSD's documentation calls MBR partitions slices):

Offset in entry Size Meaning
0 1 Boot indicator: 0x80 = active (boot this one), 0x00 = not active
1 3 First sector in packed CHS form (head, then sector/cylinder as in INT 13h)
4 1 Partition type (0x01 FAT12, 0x04 FAT16 < 32 MB, 0x06 FAT16 >= 32 MB, 0x05 extended, 0xA5 FreeBSD)
5 3 Last sector in packed CHS form
8 4 LBA of the first sector ("relative sectors")
12 4 Number of sectors

The layout is the one documented in boot0.S and written field by field by MS-DOS FDISK in write_master_boot_to_disk(). The MBR program's job is always the same: choose a partition, load that partition's first sector (its volume boot record) to 0x7C00, check its signature, and jump to it with DL still naming the drive.

Relocation: making room at 0x7C00#

There is an immediate problem. The MBR is itself running at 0x7C00, the address where the next boot sector must be loaded, because every boot sector expects to run there. So every MBR begins by copying itself somewhere else and continuing there. Both MS-DOS and FreeBSD choose linear 0x600.

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 1.2 – The MS-DOS 4.00 MBR relocates itself from 0:7C00 to 0:0600 (FDBOOT.ASM lines 12-34)Source ↗
_data   segment public
        assume  cs:_data,ds:_data

        org 600h

        cli             ;no interrupts for now
        xor ax,ax
        mov ss,ax
        mov sp,7c00h    ;new stack at 0:7c00
        mov si,sp       ;where this boot record starts - 0:7c00
        push ax
        pop es          ;seg regs the same
        push ax
        pop ds
        sti             ;interrupts ok now
        cld
        mov di,0600h    ;where to relocate this boot record to
        mov cx,100h
        repnz movsw     ;relocate to 0:0600
;       jmp entry2
        db   0eah
        dw   $+4,0
entry2:

ORG 600h tells the assembler that the code will execute at 0x600, although the BIOS loads it at 0x7C00; the first instructions use no absolute addresses, so they work at either place. repnz movsw with CX = 100h copies 256 words, the whole sector (repnz acts like rep for movsw). The jump into the copy is hand-assembled: db 0eah is the far-jump opcode and dw $+4,0 supplies offset $+4 (the 5-byte instruction's end, which is entry2 in the copy) and segment 0.

Choosing the partition#

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 1.3 – FDBOOT walks the partition table and insists on exactly one active entry (FDBOOT.ASM lines 35-55)Source ↗
        mov si,offset tab      ;partition table
        mov bl,4        ;number of table entries
next:
        cmp byte ptr[si],80h  ;is this a bootable entry?
        je boot         ;yes
        cmp byte ptr[si],0    ;no, is boot indicator zero?
        jne bad         ;no, it must be x"00" or x"80" to be valid
        add si,16       ;yes, go to next entry
        dec bl
        jnz next
        int 18h         ;no bootable entries - go to rom basic
boot:
        mov dx,[si]     ;head and drive to boot from
        mov cx,[si+2]   ;cyl, sector to boot from
        mov bp,si       ;save table entry address to pass to partition boot record
next1:
        add si,16       ;next table entry
        dec bl          ;# entries left
        jz tabok        ;all entries look ok
        cmp byte ptr[si],0    ;all remaining entries should begin with zero
        je next1        ;this one is ok

The rule is strict: an entry's first byte must be 0x80 or 0x00, and exactly one may be 0x80; anything else prints "Invalid partition table" and stops in hold: jmp hold. With no active entry the code executes INT 18h, which on the original IBM PC started ROM BASIC (hence the comment). Line 47, mov dx,[si], loads DL from the boot-indicator byte (0x80) and DH from the head byte: the MS-DOS MBR always reads from BIOS drive 0x80, whatever the BIOS passed in DL. The read that follows (lines 70-93) is attempted up to five times, with a disk reset after each failure, the loaded sector must carry the signature at 0x7DFE, and SI is left pointing at the active entry before the far jump to 0:7C00.

How FDISK carries the MBR inside FDISK.EXE#

The 512 bytes are compiled into FDISK. Its makefile assembles and links FDBOOT.ASM, converts it to a flat image with exe2bin (which, because of ORG 600h, begins with 0x600 bytes of padding), and runs dbof fdboot.bin fdboot.inc 600 200 to extract the sector as assembler db lines (FDISK/MAKEFILE lines 74-80; dbof is a build tool in v4.0/src/TOOLS). The FAT boot sector is built the same way (dbof msboot.bin boot.inc 7c00 200, BOOT/MAKEFILE). BOOTREC.ASM then includes the generated file twice, under the public label _master_boot_record. That is deliberate: the C code declares extern unsigned char master_boot_record[2][512] (GLOBAL.C), one template per fixed disk. At start-up FDISK reads each disk's sector 0 and, if it already carries the signature, copies it over the template (FDISK.C lines 719-731). So FDISK 4.00 installs its own boot code only on a disk without a valid MBR. When it writes, write_master_boot_to_disk() overwrites only the changed partition entries and forces 0x55, 0xAA into bytes 510-511.

FreeBSD's mbr.S#

FreeBSD ships two MBR programs. /boot/mbr (stand/i386/mbr/mbr.S) is a plain "boot the active partition" MBR like FDISK's; /boot/boot0 is an interactive boot manager. Their makefiles both set ORG=0x600 (mbr Makefile, boot0 Makefile), so both relocate to 0x600 as FDBOOT does. mbr.S copies only the part of itself from label main onward, then scans the table:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 1.4 – mbr.S scans all four entries and rejects more than one active partition (mbr.S lines 52-70)Source ↗
# Scan the partition table looking for an active entry.  Note that %ch is
# zero from the repeated string instruction above.  We save the offset of
# the active partition in %si and scan the entire table to ensure that only
# one partition is marked active.
#
main:           xorw %si,%si                    # No active partition
                movw $partbl,%bx                # Partition table
                movb $0x4,%cl                   # Number of entries
main.1:         cmpb %ch,(%bx)                  # Null entry?
                je main.2                       # Yes
                jg err_pt                       # If 0x1..0x7f
                testw %si,%si                   # Active already found?
                jnz err_pt                      # Yes
                movw %bx,%si                    # Point to active
main.2:         addb $0x10,%bl                  # Till
                loop main.1                     #  done
                testw %si,%si                   # Active found?
                jnz main.3                      # Yes
                int $0x18                       # BIOS: Diskless boot

The comparison cmpb %ch,(%bx) with CH = 0 uses signed arithmetic: values 0x01-0x7F are "greater" and rejected as invalid, while 0x80-0xFF are negative and accepted as active. The policy matches FDBOOT's, but FreeBSD trusts the BIOS's DL when it names an existing hard disk (the BIOS data area byte at 0x475 holds the number of hard disks) and only falls back to the table's first byte otherwise (lines 75-81). The read prefers EDD (lines 86-117): six push instructions build the 16-byte disk address packet on the stack (size 0x10, one sector, buffer offset and segment, and the 64-bit LBA from bytes 8-11 of the entry with a zero high half), and INT 13h AX=4200h reads it. The flags byte enabling this path sits just before the partition table (lines 151-155) and defaults to 0x80; in the lab's build/freebsd/boot/mbr the byte at offset 0x1BD is indeed 0x80, preceded by 0x90 (NOP) padding from .org PT_OFF-1,0x90. The three error messages are word for word those of MS-DOS's FDISK (FDISK5.SKL).

FreeBSD's boot0: a menu in 512 bytes#

boot0 does the same job interactively: it prints one line per bootable partition (F1 FreeBSD, F2 Win, …), an entry for the next disk, and waits for a key with a timeout. Its source warns that it "uses many tricks to save space and fit in one sector" (lines 37-42). The first trick is in the relocation:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 1.5 – boot0 relocates itself and builds a fake partition entry at 0x800 (boot0.S lines 172-199)Source ↗
start:          cld                             # String ops inc
                xorw %ax,%ax                    # Zero
                movw %ax,%es                    # Address
                movw %ax,%ds                    #  data
                movw %ax,%ss                    # Set up
                movw $LOAD,%sp                  #  stack

        /*
         * Copy this code to the address it was linked for, 0x600 by default.
         */
                movw %sp,%si                    # Source
                movw $start,%di                 # Destination
                movw $0x100,%cx                 # Word count
                rep                             # Relocate
                movsw                           #  code
        /*
         * After the code, (i.e. at %di+0, 0x800) create a partition entry,
         * initialized to LBA 0 / CHS 0:0:1.
         * Set %bp to point to the partition and also, with negative offsets,
         * to the variables embedded in the bootblock (nextdrv and so on).
         */
                movw %di,%bp                    # Address variables
                movb $0x8,%cl                   # Words to clear
                rep                             # Zero
                stosw                           #  them
                incb -0xe(%di)                  # Set the S field to 1

                jmp main-LOAD+ORIGIN            # Jump to relocated code

After rep movsw, DI points just past the copy, at 0x800. boot0 points BP there and zeroes 16 bytes to make a fake partition entry for CHS 0:0:1 / LBA 0, sector 0 of a disk (incb -0xe(%di) sets its sector field to 1). That entry is used for "next drive" (F5) and, as Study case 1.B shows, for writing sector 0 back. BP also reaches boot0's configuration bytes at the end of the sector through negative offsets (_FLAGS(%bp), _OPT(%bp), the .set block): a [bp-n] operand costs one displacement byte, an absolute address two.

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 1.6 – The menu loop: one line per enabled, non-empty partition (type lookup elided) (boot0.S lines 252-288)Source ↗
                movw $(partbl+0x4),%bx          # Partition table (+4)
                xorw %dx,%dx                    # Item number

        /*
         * Loop around on the partition table, printing values until we
         * pass a 256 byte boundary.
         */
read_entry:     movb %ch,-0x4(%bx)              # Zero active flag (ch == 0)
                btw %dx,_FLAGS(%bp)             # Entry enabled?
                jnc next_entry                  # No
                movb (%bx),%al                  # Load type
                test %al, %al                   # skip empty partition
                jz next_entry
⋮
                addw $(TLEN-1), %di             # Adjust
                movb (%di),%cl                  # Partition
                addw %cx,%di                    #  description
                callw putx                      # Display it

next_entry:     incw %dx                        # Next item
                addb $0x10,%bl                  # Next entry
                jnc read_entry                  # Till done

The loop starts BX at partbl+4 and adds 16 per entry; after four entries the low byte of BX overflows past a 256-byte boundary, setting the carry flag, so jnc read_entry ends the loop without a counter register. Each entry's active flag is cleared (movb %ch,-0x4(%bx)); boot0 will set it again on the entry the user picks. The elided lines look up the partition type with repne scasb in bootable_ids; a parallel table of one-byte relative offsets (desc_ofs) then finds the name string. Strings end with a byte whose bit 7 is set instead of a terminating zero, which saves one byte per string (lines 630-645).

The shipped boot0 is built with OPTS ?= -DVOLUME_SERIAL -DPXE (Makefile line 16). VOLUME_SERIAL moves the data area to 0x1AE to make room for a 4-byte Windows disk signature, and PXE adds an F6 PXE entry. To pay for them, SAVE_MEMORY and SAVE_MORE_MEMORY drop the type entries 0x01, 0x04 and 0x05 and the DOS string (lines 18-30, lines 592-645). The lab's build/freebsd/boot/boot0 confirms it: there is no DOS text in the file, so a FAT16 partition (type 0x06) is labelled Win.

boot0cfg(8): configuring the boot manager from user space#

Because boot0's options are bytes inside the sector, boot0cfg(8) can change them without reassembling anything: it reads sector 0, recognises boot0, edits the bytes at offsets it knows for each of two layouts (the b0_ofs table), and writes the sector back. boot0bs() identifies the layout by comparing the first 12 code bytes (FC 31 C0 8E C0 8E D8 8E D0 BC 00 7C, the start of Listing 1.5, also the first 12 bytes of the lab's boot0 file) and looking for Drive at 0x1B2 (original layout) or 0x1AE (volume-serial layout). The comment in boot0.S says the first instructions must never change for exactly this reason (lines 166-170). If the disk device cannot be opened for writing directly, write_mbr() falls back to asking the GEOM partition class to install the sector through its bootcode verb.

MS-DOS 4.00 FDBOOT FreeBSD mbr FreeBSD boot0
Runs at 0:0600 0:0600 0:0600
Partition choice the single 0x80 entry the single active entry user menu, default after timeout
Disk access CHS only EDD if present, else CHS EDD if flag 0x80 set, else CHS
Drive used always 0x80 (from table byte) BIOS DL if valid BIOS DL, or forced by setdrv
Writes to disk never never yes, the chosen default (see Study case 1.B)
Configured by FDISK partition table only gpart, fdisk(8) boot0cfg(8)

1.3 The volume boot record and the first stage#

The sector that the MBR loads, the first sector of a partition (or sector 0 of a floppy, which has no MBR), is the volume boot record (VBR). Here the two systems diverge completely. The MS-DOS VBR loads the operating system almost directly: it finds IO.SYS and jumps into it. FreeBSD's VBR is the first of several stages that eventually switch the processor to protected mode and run a full program loader.

MSBOOT: the FAT boot sector#

v4.0/src/BOOT/MSBOOT.ASM assembles to one 512-byte sector. FORMAT and SYS do not read it from a file: as with FDISK, the BOOT makefile turns the binary into INC\BOOT.INC, and FORMAT includes it (INCLUDE BOOT.INC, MSFOR.ASM lines 199-200), as does SYS (SYS1.ASM line 263). The sector begins with a jump over a data table, the BIOS Parameter Block (BPB), which describes the FAT file system on the medium. FAT itself (clusters, the file allocation table, directory entries) is the subject of a later module; here we only need the fields MSBOOT uses.

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 1.7 – The extended BPB at the start of the MS-DOS 4.00 boot sector (MSBOOT.ASM lines 98-129)Source ↗
;J.K. Extened_BPB

if ibmcopyright
          DB      "IBM  "
else
          DB      "MSDOS"
endif
          DB      "4.0"                 ;AN005;
ByteSec   DW      cbSec                 ; SIZE OF A PHYSICAL SECTOR
          DB      8                     ; SECTORS PER ALLOCATION UNIT
cSecRes   DW      1                     ; NUMBER OF RESERVED SECTORS
cFat      DB      2                     ; NUMBER OF FATS
DirNum    DW      512                   ; NUMBER OF DIREC ENTRIES
cTotSec   DW      4*17*305-1            ; NUMBER OF SECTORS - NUMBER OF HIDDEN SECTORS
                                        ;  (0 when 32 bit sector number)
MEDIA     DB      0F8H                  ; MEDIA BYTE
cSecFat   DW      8                     ; NUMBER OF FAT SECTORS
SECLIM    DW      17                    ; SECTORS PER TRACK
HDLIM     DW      4                     ; NUMBER OF SURFACES
Ext_cSecHid label dword
cSecHid_L DW      1                     ;AN000; NUMBER OF HIDDEN SECTORS
cSecHid_H dw      0                     ;AN000; high order word of Hiden Sectors
Ext_cTotSec label dword
ctotsec_L dw      0                     ;AN000; 32 bit version of NUMBER OF SECTORS
ctotsec_H dw      0                     ;AN000; (when 16 bit version is zero)
;
Phydrv    db     80h                    ;AN004;
Curhd     db      0h                    ;AN004; Current Head
Ext_Boot_Sig    db    41                ;AN000;
Boot_Serial     dd    0                 ;AN000;
Boot_Vol_Label  db    'NO NAME    '     ;AN000;
Boot_System_id  db    'FAT12   '        ;AN000;

The values assembled here (0F8h media byte, 17 sectors per track, 4 heads, 4*17*305-1 sectors) describe a small hard disk and are only defaults. FORMAT copies the real BPB of the medium over them before writing the sector (WriteBootSector) and patches Phydrv to 00h for floppies or 80h for hard disks (MSFOR.ASM lines 299-310). Everything from Ext_cSecHid on is new in 4.00: 32-bit hidden and total sector counts for partitions larger than 32 MB, the drive number, an extended boot signature (decimal 41, which is 29h), a volume serial number, a volume label and a file-system name. The same layout is declared as a structure, EXT_IBMBOOT_HEADER, in INC\BOOTFORM.INC, which FORMAT, SYS and MSLOAD share. Study case 1.A gives every field's byte offset.

The first instructions set up a stack just below the sector (SS:SP = 0000:7C00, lines 151-158) and then patch the floppy controller's parameter table (lines 167-192). Interrupt vector 1Eh is not code: the BIOS uses it as a pointer to an 11-byte diskette parameter table. MSBOOT copies that table into its own sector, sets the head-settle time and the end-of-track value (the last sector number of a track, taken from SECLIM in the BPB), and points vector 1Eh at the copy. The original vector stays on the stack for the error path. Then INT 13h with AX = 0 resets the disk system, using the DL the BIOS passed. The copy's destination, Sec9, is UDATA+0, which is the address of START itself: the table overwrites instructions that have already executed. The assembler-time check if $ le BIOS$_L prints a warning (%OUT Don't destroy unexcuted code yet!!!) during assembly if this trick would ever overwrite code that has not run yet; %OUT only prints a message, so it does not stop the build (the lab build does not print it).

Next MSBOOT computes where the root directory and the data area begin, in 32-bit arithmetic (DX:AX):

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 1.8 – Computing the first root-directory sector and the first data sector (MSBOOT.ASM lines 209-235)Source ↗
        xor     ax,ax                   ;AN000;
        cmp     cTotSec,ax              ;AN000; 32 bit calculation?
        je      Dir_Cont                ;AN000;
        mov     cx,cTotSec              ;AN000;
        mov     cTotSec_L,cx            ;AN000; cTotSec_L,cTotSec_H will be used for calculation
Dir_Cont:                               ;AN000;
        MOV     AL,cFat                 ;Determine sector dir starts on
        MUL     cSecFat                 ;DX;AX
        ADD     AX,cSecHid_L
        adc     DX,cSecHid_H            ;AN000;
        ADD     AX,cSecRes
        ADC     DX,0
        MOV     [DIR$_L],AX             ; DX;AX = cFat*cSecFat + cSecRes + cSecHid
        mov     [DIR$_H],DX             ;AN000;
        MOV     [BIOS$_L],AX
        mov     [BIOS$_H],DX            ;AN000;
;
; Take into account size of directory (only know number of directory entries)
;
        MOV     AX,cbDirEnt             ; bytes per directory entry
        MUL     DirNum                  ; convert to bytes in directory
        MOV     BX,ByteSec              ; add in sector size
        ADD     AX,BX
        DEC     AX                      ; decrement so that we round up
        DIV     BX                      ; convert to sector number
        ADD     [BIOS$_L],AX            ; Start sector # of Data area
        adc     [BIOS$_H],0             ;AN000;

In formula form, with all numbers taken from the BPB:

DIR$  = cSecHid + cSecRes + cFat * cSecFat
BIOS$ = DIR$ + ceil(DirNum * 32 / ByteSec)

For a 1.44 MB floppy (1 reserved sector, 2 FATs of 9 sectors, 224 root entries, no hidden sectors) that is DIR$ = 19 and BIOS$ = 19 + 14 = 33. The variable is called BIOS$ because the first data sector is where IO.SYS, the "DOS BIOS", must begin.

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 1.9 – Reading the first directory sector to 0:0500 and checking the first two names (MSBOOT.ASM lines 243-268)Source ↗
        MOV     BX,DirOff               ; sector to go in at 00500h
        mov     dx,[DIR$_H]             ;AN000;
        MOV     AX,[DIR$_L]             ; logical sector of directory
        CALL    DODIV                   ; convert to sector, track, head
        jc      CKErr                   ;AN000; Overflow? BPB must be wrong!!
;        MOV     AX,0201H                ; disk read 1 sector
        mov     al, 1                   ;AN000; disk read 1 sector
        CALL    DOCALL                  ; do the disk read
        JB      CKERR                   ; if errors try to recover
;
; Now we scan for the presence of IBMBIO  COM and IBMDOS  COM.  Check the
; first directory entry.
;
        MOV     DI,BX
        MOV     CX,11
        MOV     SI,OFFSET BIO           ; point to "ibmbio  com"
        REPZ    CMPSB                   ; see if the same
        JNZ     CKERR                   ; if not there advise the user
;
; Found the BIOS.  Check the second directory entry.
;
        LEA     DI,[BX+20h]
        MOV     SI,OFFSET DOS           ; point to "ibmdos  com"
        MOV     CX,11
        REPZ    CMPSB
        JZ      DoLoad

MSBOOT reads one directory sector to linear 0x500 and compares the first two 32-byte directory entries with the 11-character names BIO and DOS. The comments still say IBMBIO COM and IBMDOS COM, but the names actually assembled depend on a build switch (lines 500-506): IBMBIO COM/IBMDOS COM if IBMCOPYRIGHT, otherwise IO SYS/MSDOS SYS. IBMCOPYRIGHT is set to FALSE in INC\VERSION.INC, so this tree builds the Microsoft names IO.SYS and MSDOS.SYS. That matches the rest of the build: the BIOS makefile produces io.sys (dest = io, line 3), and CPY.BAT copies bios\io.sys and dos\msdos.sys. In a boot sector assembled from this tree, the 22 bytes IO SYSMSDOS SYS sit at offsets 0x1DB-0x1F0.

If either name does not match, or a read fails, MSBOOT prints "Non-System disk or disk error / Replace and press any key when ready" (from USA-MS.MSG via BOOT.SKL), waits for a key, restores vector 1Eh, and executes INT 19h to restart the BIOS boot (lines 274-282). There are no retries.

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 1.10 – Loading the first three sectors of IO.SYS to 0070:0000 and jumping there (MSBOOT.ASM lines 301-411)Source ↗
DoLoad:
        mov     BX,BioOff               ;offset of ibmbio(IBMLOAD) to be loaded.
        mov     CX,IBMLOADSIZE          ;# of sectors to read.
        mov     AX, [BIOS$_L]           ;Sector number to read.
        mov     DX, [BIOS$_H]           ;AN000;
Do_While:                               ;AN000;
        push    AX                      ;AN000;
        push    DX                      ;AN000;
        push    CX                      ;AN000;
        call    DODIV                   ;AN000; DX;AX = sector number.
        jc      Load_Failure            ;AN000; Adjust stack. Show error message
        mov     al, 1                   ;AN000; Read 1 sector at a time.
                                        ;This is to handle a case of media
                                        ;when the first sector of IBMLOAD is the
                                        ;the last sector in a track.
        call    DOCALL                  ;AN000; Read the sector.
        pop     CX                      ;AN000;
        pop     DX                      ;AN000;
        pop     AX                      ;AN000;
        jc      CkErr                   ;AN000; Read error?
        add     AX,1                    ;AN000; Next sector number.
        adc     DX,0                    ;AN000;
        add     BX,ByteSec              ;AN000; adjust buffer address.
        loop    Do_While                ;AN000;
⋮
DISKOK:
        MOV     CH,Media
        MOV     DL,PhyDrv
        MOV     bx,[BIOS$_L]            ;AN000; J.K.I1.Get bios sector in bx
        mov     ax,[BIOS$_H]            ;AN000; J.K.I1.
        JMP     FAR PTR BIOS            ;CRANK UP THE DOS

Only IBMLOADSIZE = 3 sectors are loaded, one at a time, starting at the first data sector, to 0000:0700. MSBOOT never looks at the FAT or at the starting-cluster field of the directory entry; it simply assumes that IO.SYS begins in the first data cluster and that its first three sectors are contiguous. Those three sectors hold MSLOAD, a second-stage loader that knows how to follow the FAT (Section 1.4). The far jump to BIOS, declared as SEGBIOS SEGMENT AT BIOSEG with BIOSEG EQU 70H, goes to 0070:0000, the same byte as 0000:0700. The hand-off registers are CH = media byte, DL = Phydrv (the drive number FORMAT stored, not the one the BIOS passed), and AX:BX = the 32-bit first data sector.

These choices produce the well-known constraints on a bootable MS-DOS disk, and each one is visible in the code:

  1. IO.SYS and MSDOS.SYS must be the first two entries of the root directory (the two REPZ CMPSB comparisons).
  2. IO.SYS must start at the first data sector, and its first three sectors must be contiguous (the DoLoad loop reads from BIOS$ without consulting the FAT).
  3. MSLOAD must fit in three sectors; IBMLOADSIZE must agree in MSBOOT and in BOOTFORM.INC (the comment in BOOTFORM.INC says so). In the lab build, MSLOAD.COM is 1,247 bytes.
  4. The high word of every sector number must be smaller than the number of sectors per track, or DODIV refuses with the carry flag set to avoid a divide overflow. Study case 1.A works out what that means for where a bootable partition may start: its root directory and first data sectors must lie below sector SECLIM x 65536 of the disk.

This is why SYS.COM exists: an ordinary COPY does not place files at the start of the directory and of the data area.

FreeBSD boot1: the first sector of the slice#

On an MBR-partitioned disk, FreeBSD keeps a 16-sector boot block at the start of its slice: the file /boot/boot, which is boot1 (512 bytes) followed by boot2 (7,680 bytes). The Makefile builds it with cat boot1 boot2 > boot and pads boot2 to BOOT2SIZE= 7680 (boot2 Makefile lines 44-63); in build/freebsd/boot/ the three files are 512, 7,680 and 8,192 bytes long. Like the MS-DOS sector, boot1 starts with a jump and a BPB, but an empty one: the comment explains that some IBM firmware ("El Torito emulation") writes into the BPB area of the loaded sector, so FreeBSD reserves those bytes to keep the firmware from corrupting code (lines 43-78). MS-DOS conventions had become part of the PC platform. boot1 then copies itself to 0x700 (that copy's xread routine is used later by boot2). Unlike MSBOOT, it does not trust a stored partition location: it re-reads the MBR and makes two passes over the table, first for an active slice of type 0xA5, then for any slice of that type (lines 136-167). Then it loads 16 sectors and starts the next stage:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 1.11 – boot1 loads boot1+boot2, moves the boot2 client, enables A20 and jumps into BTX (boot1.S lines 186-218)Source ↗
main.5:         mov %dx,MEM_ARG                 # Save args
                movb $NSECT,%dh                 # Sector count
                callw nread                     # Read disk
                mov $MEM_BTX,%bx                # BTX
                mov 0xa(%bx),%si                # Get BTX length and set
                add %bx,%si                     #  %si to start of boot2.bin
                mov $MEM_USR+SIZ_PAG*2,%di      # Client page 2
                mov $MEM_BTX+(NSECT-1)*SIZ_SEC,%cx # Byte
                sub %si,%cx                     #  count
                rep                             # Relocate
                movsb                           #  client
⋮
seta20:         cli                             # Disable interrupts
seta20.1:       dec %cx                         # Timeout?
                jz seta20.3                     # Yes
                inb $0x64,%al                   # Get status
                testb $0x2,%al                  # Busy?
                jnz seta20.1                    # Yes
                movb $0xd1,%al                  # Command: Write
                outb %al,$0x64                  #  output port
seta20.2:       inb $0x64,%al                   # Get status
                testb $0x2,%al                  # Busy?
                jnz seta20.2                    # Yes
                movb $0xdf,%al                  # Enable
                outb %al,$0x60                  #  A20
seta20.3:       sti                             # Enable interrupts

                jmp start+MEM_JMP-MEM_ORG       # Start BTX

Three details deserve comment. The 16 sectors land at 0x8C00; since the first is boot1 itself and the second a 512-byte disk-label sector, BTX begins exactly at 0x9000, its link address. The boot2 client is copied to 0xC000, which is MEM_USR + 0x2000, the address btxld -E 0x2000 linked it for. And the code opens the A20 gate: the 8086 wrapped addresses above 1 MB back to 0, and the IBM AT kept that behaviour by gating address line 20 through the keyboard controller (command 0xD1 to port 0x64, then 0xDF to port 0x60). Protected-mode code that wants memory above 1 MB must open the gate. The MS-DOS 4.00 boot path (BOOT, BIOS and DOS directories) contains no A20 code at all; it has no use for memory above 1 MB at boot time.

boot2: a UFS reader that runs as a BTX client#

boot2.c is C code, compiled for 32-bit protected mode, that must still fit in a few kilobytes. It knows the UFS file system (it includes ufsread.c), the MBR and BSD disk labels, and the ELF and a.out executable formats. Its main() (boot2.c lines 198-246) reads an optional configuration file, then loads the third stage unless a key is pressed. PATH_CONFIG, PATH_DOTCONFIG and PATH_LOADER are /boot/config, /boot.config and /boot/loader (stand/common/paths.h); PATH_KERNEL is /boot/kernel/kernel (sys/sys/boot.h). If the user presses a key within about three seconds, or loading /boot/loader fails, boot2 prints its boot: prompt and can load a kernel directly. Note ARGS = 0x900: boot1 left the drive number and slice there (mov %dx,MEM_ARG).

How does protected-mode C code read a disk through a real-mode BIOS? It asks BTX:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 1.12 – boot2 reads sectors by asking BTX to far-call xread in the relocated boot1 (boot2.c lines 580-603)Source ↗
static int
drvread(void *buf, unsigned lba, unsigned nblk)
{
        static unsigned c = 0x2d5c7c2f;

        if (!OPT_CHECK(RBX_QUIET)) {
                xputc(c = c << 8 | c >> 24);
                xputc('\b');
        }
        v86.ctl = V86_ADDR | V86_CALLF | V86_FLAGS;
        v86.addr = XREADORG;            /* call to xread in boot1 */
        v86.es = VTOPSEG(buf);
        v86.eax = lba;
        v86.ebx = VTOPOFF(buf);
        v86.ecx = lba >> 16;
        v86.edx = nblk << 8 | dsk.drive;
        v86int();
        v86.ctl = V86_FLAGS;
        if (V86_CY(v86.efl)) {
                printf("error %u lba %u\n", v86.eax >> 8 & 0xff, lba);
                return (-1);
        }
        return (0);
}

The v86 structure holds the registers for a real-mode call; V86_CALLF asks for a far call to the real-mode address XREADORG, which the Makefile computes from the location of xread in boot1 relocated to 0x700 (Makefile lines 85-90). boot2 prints characters the same way, with v86.addr = 0x10 for INT 10h (putc()).

BTX: a tiny protected-mode kernel for boot programs#

BTX ("boot extender") is a tiny kernel that runs at 0x9000 (its header carries the magic BTX, btx.S lines 115-126). It switches the processor to 32-bit protected mode by setting bit 0 of CR0, then starts one client program (boot2, gptboot, or the loader) in ring 3 by building an interrupt frame and executing IRET (lines 188-234). It offers the client two services: INT 30h (exit, or exec a new program in ring 0) and INT 31h (call a real-mode BIOS routine). The client's code and data segments have their base at MEM_USR = 0xA000 and privilege level 3 (the GDT: descriptors with access bytes 0xFA and 0xF2). So a client pointer p refers to linear address p + 0xA000; this is why boot2 and the loader use the PTOV() and VTOP() macros (btxv86.h). The initial stack pointer is computed from the BIOS memory size at BDA 0x413.

The interesting part is INT 31h. The library routine __v86int loads the registers from the v86 structure and executes int $0x31 (btxv86.S). BTX's handler then does something you might not expect from the names:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 1.13 – BTX leaves protected mode to run the BIOS routine in real mode (btx.S lines 563-584)Source ↗
intusr.6:       movl -0x08(%esi),%ebx           # Copy user flags to real
                movl %ebx,MEM_ESPR-0x0c         #  mode return trampoline
                movl $rret_tramp,%ebx           # Set return trampoline
                movl %ebx,MEM_ESPR-0x10         #  CS:IP
                movl %eax,MEM_ESPR-0x16         # Real mode target CS:IP
                ljmpw $SEL_RCODE,$intusr.7      # Change to 16-bit segment
                .code16
intusr.7:       movl %cr0,%eax                  # Leave
                dec %al                         #  protected
                movl %eax,%cr0                  #  mode
                ljmpw $0x0,$intusr.8
intusr.8:       xorw %ax,%ax                    # Reset %ds
                movw %ax,%ds                    #  and
                movw %ax,%ss                    #  %ss
                lidt ivtdesc                    # Set IVT
                popl %es                        # Restore
                popl %ds                        #  seg
                popl %fs                        #  regs
                popl %gs
                popal                           # Restore gp regs
                movw $MEM_ESPR-0x16,%sp         # Switch to real mode stack
                iret                            # Call target routine

The code clears the protection-enable bit in CR0 (dec %al), reloads the real-mode IVT, and IRETs into the BIOS routine with a return address pointing at rret_tramp, which re-enters protected mode and restores the result registers to the client (the segment registers through btx_v86); the library's __v86int then stores them in the client's v86 structure (lines 607-689). Hardware interrupts that arrive while the client runs are handled the same way: BTX reprograms the interrupt controllers so IRQs arrive at vectors 0x20-0x2F (setpic) and reflects each one to the BIOS handler in real mode (lines 394-428).

A note on terminology: the interface is called "V86" (struct __v86, V86_CALLF, the message "Invalid VM86 Request"), which suggests virtual 8086 mode, a protected-mode sub-mode in which 8086 code runs under a monitor. The 15.1 source does not use that mode. Nothing in btx.S sets the PSL_VM flag; the constant is only tested when printing a register dump (line 738). BIOS calls are made by switching the CPU back to real mode, as Listing 1.13 shows. When you read older material, check it against the pinned source.

gptboot: the same idea for GPT disks#

On a disk with a GUID Partition Table (GPT), sector 0 holds a protective MBR, /boot/pmbr, whose code (pmbr.S lines 98-162) reads the GPT header (signature EFI PART) and loads the freebsd-boot partition (up to 545 KB: it stops at 0x90000). That partition contains gptboot, the GPT counterpart of boot1+boot2. gptboot(8) describes how it picks a freebsd-ufs partition, honouring the bootme and bootonce attributes, before loading /boot/loader exactly as boot2 does. The lab's gptboot file is 61,859 bytes (btxld combines gptldr.S, the C program and BTX, gptboot Makefile lines 43-61) and can include features boot2 lacks, such as GELI disk-encryption support. Study case 1.B returns to gptboot, because it also writes to the disk during boot.

1.4 Second stage and kernel initialisation#

MS-DOS: from MSLOAD to COMMAND.COM#

IO.SYS is two programs glued together. The BIOS makefile links the resident BIOS and the initialisation code into msbio.bin, then prepends the loader: copy /b msload.com+msbio.bin $(dest).sys (BIOS/MAKEFILE lines 156-166). The link order in MSBIO.LNK puts the resident device drivers first and the initialisation code (MSINIT, SYSINIT1, SYSCONF, SYSINIT2, SYSIMES) last, so that the latter can be discarded.

Step 1, MSLOAD. MSBOOT jumped to the first byte of MSLOAD at 0070:0000. MSLOAD must load the rest of IO.SYS to that same address, overwriting itself, so it first asks INT 12h for the memory size, reserves a one-sector FAT buffer at the top, copies itself just below it, and "returns" into the copy with a far RET after pushing the new CS:IP (MSLOAD.ASM lines 240-265), a common 8086 idiom for an indirect far jump. It then reads the BPB from the boot sector still at 0:7C00, follows the FAT chain of IO.SYS (reading FAT sectors only as they are needed), loads each further cluster after the part already in memory, and finally jumps to 0070:0000 with the same register contract MSBOOT used (GO_IBMBIO). The header comment lists what this design fixed in 4.00: IO.SYS no longer has to be contiguous, and its size is no longer limited to 29 KB (lines 1-23; the title on line 3 is "Non-Contiguous IBMBIO Loader").

Step 2, the BIOS INIT. The first instruction of the resident BIOS is JMP INIT (MSBDATA.INC). INIT in BIOS/MSINIT.ASM saves and replaces the INT 13h and INT 19h vectors (lines 421-450), asks the BIOS for equipment and memory size (INT 11h, INT 12h), sets up the resident drivers' tables, and computes two segment addresses: CURRENT_DOS_LOCATION, where MSDOS.SYS will be read now (just past the BIOS and SYSINIT), and FINAL_DOS_LOCATION, where it will live (just past the resident part of the BIOS). Then it loads MSDOS.SYS, using a sector MSBOOT left behind:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 1.14 – MSINIT finds MSDOS.SYS through the directory sector MSBOOT left at 0:0500 (MSINIT.ASM lines 1368-1392)Source ↗
;       THE BOOT PROGRAM HAS LEFT THE DIRECTORY AT 0:500

        PUSH    DS
        XOR     DI,DI
        MOV     DS,DI                   ; ES:DI POINTS TO LOAD LOCATION
        MOV     BX,DS:WORD PTR [53AH]   ;   CLUS=*53A;
        POP     DS                      ;
⋮
        ADD     AX,CODE

        MOV     ES,AX                   ;
        CALL    GETCLUS                 ;       CLUS = GETCLUS (CLUS);

53Ah is 500h + 20h + 1Ah: the starting-cluster field (offset 1Ah) of the second directory entry (offset 20h) in the sector MSBOOT read to 0:0500. The boot sector's leftovers are part of the interface between stages. MSINIT follows the FAT chain with GETCLUS until an end-of-chain marker (0FF7h or higher for FAT12, 0FFF7h for FAT16) and then executes JMP SYSINIT (lines 1394-1411).

Step 3, SYSINIT moves things into place. SYSINIT (in BIOS/SYSINIT1.ASM) is a relocating initialiser: it runs from wherever it is, moves itself out of the way, and then rearranges memory.

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 1.15 – SYSINIT relocates itself to the top of memory, moves MSDOS.SYS down, and calls DOSINIT (SYSINIT1.ASM lines 460-512)Source ↗
        MOV     AX,OFFSET SYSSIZE
        Call    ParaRound
        SUB     CX,AX                   ;Compute new sysinit location
        MOV     ES,CX
        MOV     CX,OFFSET SYSSIZE + 1
        SHR     CX,1                    ;Divide by 2 to get words
        REP     MOVSW                   ;RELOCATE SYSINIT
⋮
        MOV     AX,[CURRENT_DOS_LOCATION]   ; Where it is (set by BIOS)
        MOV     DS,AX
        MOV     AX,[FINAL_DOS_LOCATION]     ; Where it is going (set by BIOS)
        MOV     ES,AX

        ASSUME  ES:NOTHING

        XOR     SI,SI
        MOV     DI,SI

        MOV     CX,DOSSIZE/2
        REP     MOVSW

        LDS     SI,[DEVICE_LIST]        ; Set for call to DOSINIT
        MOV     DX,[MEMORY_SIZE]        ; Set for call to DOSINIT
⋮
        MOV     SP,OFFSET LOCSTACK      ; Set stack
⋮
LOCSTACK LABEL BYTE

        CALL    MSDOS                   ; Call DOSINIT

The first block copies SYSINIT to the top of memory and continues there with the same far-RET trick as MSLOAD. The second moves the DOS kernel down from CURRENT_DOS_LOCATION to FINAL_DOS_LOCATION, a fixed DOSSIZE = 0A000h bytes (40 KB, line 66) whatever the file's size, overwriting the original copy of SYSINIT. The stack is set to LOCSTACK, a label placed after the code that has just run, so the stack grows down over instructions that will never execute again. Finally CALL MSDOS performs a far call into the kernel's initialisation entry, DOSINIT, passing the head of the BIOS device-driver list in DS:SI and the memory size in DX.

DOSINIT (DOS/MSINIT.ASM lines 170-191) lives in a segment of class LAST, which the comment says "MUST appear last in the link map": once it returns, its own code becomes free memory. It initialises the character devices, builds the drive parameter blocks for the block devices, and installs the DOS interrupt vectors, including INT 21h, the system-call entry point that Module 2 studies (lines 469-476: addr_int_command is vector 21h according to INC\VECTOR.INC).

Step 4, CONFIG.SYS and the shell. Back in SYSINIT, DOS system calls now work, and SYSINIT uses them like an application: it allocates memory, opens files and reads \CONFIG.SYS (DOCONF, SYSCONF.ASM lines 599-614). It processes the file in several passes (Section 1.5), possibly loads SHARE.EXE, frees its temporary memory, and finally starts the shell:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 1.16 – SYSINIT starts the command interpreter with INT 21h function 4Bh (EXEC) (SYSINIT1.ASM lines 828-849)Source ↗
OKLD:
        MOV     AH,CLOSE
        INT     21H                     ; Close file
        POP     DX                      ; Recover pointer to name
        PUSH    CS
        POP     ES
        ASSUME  ES:SYSINITSEG
        MOV     BX,OFFSET COMEXE        ; Point to EXEC block
        MOV     WORD PTR [BX.EXEC0_COM_LINE+2],CS       ; Set segments
        MOV     WORD PTR [BX.EXEC0_5C_FCB+2],CS
        MOV     WORD PTR [BX.EXEC0_6C_FCB+2],CS
        XOR     AX,AX                   ;Load and go
        MOV     AH,EXEC
        STC                             ;IN CASE OF INT 24
        INT     21H                     ;GO START UP COMMAND
        ENDIF
; NOTE FALL THROUGH IF EXEC RETURNS (an error)

COMERR:
        MOV     DX,OFFSET BADCOM        ;WANT TO PRINT COMMAND ERROR
        INVOKE  BADFIL
STALL:  JMP     STALL

The program is COMMND, which defaults to \COMMAND.COM (SYSINIT2.ASM line 1493) and can be changed with SHELL=; the default command line is /P (COMMAND_LINE, line 279, where the / is replaced by the current switch character), which tells COMMAND.COM that it is the permanent, primary shell. EXEC with AL = 0 means "load and run". If it ever returns, the shell could not be started: SYSINIT prints an error and spins in STALL: JMP STALL. When the EXEC succeeds, COMMAND.COM is the first user program and this module's story on the MS-DOS side ends. How EXEC builds a process is part of Module 2.

FreeBSD: the loader#

/boot/loader is a BTX client, just like boot2, but much larger: its Makefile links it with btxld against the BTX loader and kernel (loader Makefile lines 113-120) and refuses to build if the binary exceeds LOADERSIZE = 500,000 bytes, because the loader, BTX and their stacks must fit in the 640 KB below the video memory (lines 20-40). Even in 2026, FreeBSD's BIOS boot path works inside the same 640 KB that MS-DOS 4.00 had.

The loader's C main() (stand/i386/loader/main.c) sizes memory through the BIOS, sets up a heap and consoles, probes disks and PCI, and calls interact(), which starts the scripting interpreter. In FreeBSD 15.1 the default interpreter is Lua (LOADER_DEFAULT_INTERP?=lua when Lua is enabled, stand/defs.mk); the lab's /boot/loader and /boot/loader_lua files are identical (same SHA-256). The script it runs is short:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 1.17 – loader.lua reads the configuration and either shows the menu or loads the kernel (loader.lua lines 34-59)Source ↗
require("cli")
local color = require("color")
local core = require("core")
local config = require("config")
local password = require("password")

config.load()

if core.isUEFIBoot() then
        loader.perform("efi-autoresizecons")
end
-- Our console may have been setup with different settings before we get
-- here, so make sure we reset everything back to default.
if color.isEnabled() then
        printc(core.KEYSTR_RESET)
end
try_include("local")
password.check()
if not core.isMenuSkipped() then
        require("menu").run()
else
        -- Load kernel/modules before we go
        config.loadelf()
        -- Load platform entropy if possible
        core.loadEntropy()
end

config.load() reads the files named in loader_conf_files; the defaults file sets kernel="kernel" (the directory under /boot) and loader_conf_files="/boot/device.hints /boot/loader.conf" (stand/defaults/loader.conf). Every name_load="YES" line marks a module for loading (the pattern in config.lua), and loadModule() turns each one into a load command. The loader reads the kernel ELF file and the modules into memory itself; the kernel does not need any disk driver to obtain its first modules. The menu's boot entry, or the autoboot timeout, finally executes the kernel through elf64_exec(), the handler for 64-bit ELF files (elf64_freebsd.c lines 69-118). It calls bi_load64(), builds minimal page tables, and leaves through a trampoline. bi_load64() (bootinfo64.c) packs everything the kernel must know into a module metadata list placed after the last loaded file: for each file a name, a type, an address and a size, plus, for the kernel, the boot flags (MODINFOMD_HOWTO), a pointer to a copy of the loader's environment variables (MODINFOMD_ENVP), the BIOS memory map and the end address. The record types are defined in sys/sys/linker.h. modulep is the physical address of that list. The page tables map every 1 GB slot of the 64-bit address space onto the first gigabyte of physical memory with 2 MB pages, crude but enough for the kernel, linked at a high virtual address, to start running. Then __exec() (BTX's INT 30h exec service) calls the trampoline in ring 0:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 1.18 – amd64_tramp switches from 32-bit protected mode to 64-bit long mode and jumps to the kernel (amd64_tramp.S lines 77-111)Source ↗
        /* Turn on EFER.LME */
        movl    $MSR_EFER, %ecx
        rdmsr
        orl     $EFER_LME, %eax
        wrmsr
⋮
        /* Set %cr3 for PT4 */
        movl    $VTOP(PT4), %eax
        movl    %eax, %cr3

        /* Turn on paging (implicitly sets EFER.LMA) */
        movl    %cr0, %eax
        orl     $CR0_PG, %eax
        movl    %eax, %cr0
⋮
        lgdt    (%eax)
        ljmp    $0x8, $VTOP(longmode)

        .code64
longmode:
        /* We're still running V=P, jump to entry point */
        movl    %esi, %eax
        salq    $32, %rax
        orq     %rdi, %rax
        pushq   %rax
        ret

This is the standard sequence for entering long mode: set EFER.LME, enable physical address extension in CR4 (elided lines 83-86), load CR3 with the top-level page table, and enable paging in CR0, which activates long mode in a 32-bit compatibility segment. A far jump to a 64-bit code segment (0x00209800 in the GDT: the L bit set) completes the switch, and pushq %rax; ret jumps to the 64-bit entry address. The VTOP macro adds 0xA000, BTX's client base, because this code was linked as a BTX client but runs with flat ring-0 segments.

FreeBSD: kernel entry, hammer_time() and mi_startup()#

The kernel's ELF entry point is btext in locore.S:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 1.19 – btext: the first kernel instructions on amd64 (locore.S lines 54-88)Source ↗
 * We are called with the stack looking like this:
 * 0(%rsp) = 32 bit return address (cannot be used)
 * 4(%rsp) = 32 bit modulep
 * 8(%rsp) = 32 bit kernend
 *
 * We are already in long mode, on a 64 bit %cs and running at KERNBASE.
 */
ENTRY(btext)

        /* Don't trust what the loader gives for rflags. */
        pushq   $PSL_KERNEL
        popfq

        /* Get onto a stack that we can trust - there is no going back now. */
        movq    %rsp, %rbp
        movq    $bootstack,%rsp

⋮
        /* Grab metadata pointers from the loader. */
        movl    4(%rbp),%edi            /* modulep (arg 1) */
        movl    8(%rbp),%esi            /* kernend (arg 2) */
        xorq    %rbp, %rbp

        call    hammer_time             /* set up cpu for unix operation */
        movq    %rax,%rsp               /* set up kstack for mi_startup() */
        call    mi_startup              /* autoconfiguration, mountroot etc */
0:      hlt
        jmp     0b

The two 32-bit arguments are still on the stack exactly where the trampoline left them, after the 32-bit return address pushed by BTX's call. btext passes them in %rdi/%rsi (the first two argument registers of the amd64 calling convention) to hammer_time(), the machine-dependent initialisation in sys/amd64/amd64/machdep.c. "Hammer" was AMD's code name for its first 64-bit processors.

hammer_time() begins by calling init_ops.parse_preload_data(modulep) (machdep.c lines 1292-1318), which points preload_metadata at the list built by bi_load64() and extracts the boot flags and the kernel environment (native_parse_preload_data()), so loader.conf settings are visible from the kernel's first C function. It then stores 0x1234 at 0x472 for a BIOS boot: the BIOS data area's warm-boot flag, which boot1 also sets before it reboots (boot1.S line 242). The rest of hammer_time() (lines 1320-1625) identifies the CPU, builds the GDT, IDT and TSS, initialises the console and physical memory (getmemsize()), and returns the kernel stack of thread0, the first kernel thread. btext switches to that stack and calls mi_startup(), the machine-independent ("mi") start-up in sys/kern/init_main.c:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 1.20 – mi_startup() sorts the SYSINIT list and calls every entry in order (init_main.c lines 258-335)Source ↗
void
mi_startup(void)
{
⋮
        /* Construct and sort sysinit list. */
        sysinit_mklist(&sysinit_list, SET_BEGIN(sysinit_set), SET_LIMIT(sysinit_set));
⋮
        /*
         * Perform each system initialization task from the ordered list.  Note
         * that if sysinit_list is modified (e.g. by a KLD) we will nonetheless
         * always perform the earlist-sorted sysinit at each step; using the
         * STAILQ_FOREACH macro would result in items being skipped if inserted
         * earlier than the "current item".
         */
        while ((sip = STAILQ_FIRST(&sysinit_list)) != NULL) {
                STAILQ_REMOVE_HEAD(&sysinit_list, next);
                STAILQ_INSERT_TAIL(&sysinit_done_list, sip, next);

                if (sip->subsystem == SI_SUB_DUMMY)
                        continue;       /* skip dummy task(s)*/
⋮
                /* Call function */
                (*(sip->func))(sip->udata);

#if defined(VERBOSE_SYSINIT)
                if (verbose)
                        printf("done.\n");
#endif

                /* Check off the one we're just done */
                last = sip->subsystem;
        }

That loop is the whole kernel start-up: every subsystem, from the console banner to the virtual-memory system, the scheduler and device drivers, is a SYSINIT entry in one sorted list. Section 1.5 explains where the list comes from.

FreeBSD: creating and starting init#

The first user process is also created by SYSINIT entries. create_init() runs at SI_SUB_CREATE_INIT: it calls fork1() on thread0 to make process 1, stopped (RFSTOPPED), and arranges for it to run start_init() in kernel mode when it is first scheduled (create_init()). Much later, at SI_SUB_KTHREAD_INIT, kick_init() makes it runnable (kick_init()). When process 1 runs, start_init() mounts the root file system and turns itself into the first user program:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 1.21 – start_init() tries each path in init_path until kern_execve() succeeds (init_main.c lines 763-812)Source ↗
        free_init_path = tmp_init_path = strdup(init_path, M_TEMP);

        while ((path = strsep(&tmp_init_path, ":")) != NULL) {
                if (bootverbose)
                        printf("start_init: trying %s\n", path);
⋮
                memset(td->td_frame, 0, sizeof(*td->td_frame));
                oldvmspace = p->p_vmspace;
                error = kern_execve(td, &args, NULL, oldvmspace);
                KASSERT(error != 0,
                    ("kern_execve returned success, not EJUSTRETURN"));
                if (error == EJUSTRETURN) {
                        exec_cleanup(td, oldvmspace);
                        free(free_init_path, M_TEMP);
                        TSEXIT();
                        return;
                }
                if (error != ENOENT)
                        printf("exec %s: error %d\n", path, error);
        }
        free(free_init_path, M_TEMP);
        printf("init: not found in path %s\n", init_path);
        panic("no init");
}

The default init_path is /sbin/init:/sbin/oinit:/sbin/init.bak:/rescue/init (lines 702-712), and the loader variable init_path can override it. A successful kern_execve() returns EJUSTRETURN: the process's address space has been replaced by /sbin/init, and when this kernel function returns, the thread "returns" to user mode at the program's entry point. If no candidate can be executed, the kernel panics with "no init". This is the FreeBSD counterpart of SYSINIT's EXEC of COMMAND.COM in Listing 1.16, and the end of this module's story. What execve does in detail, and what init(8) does next, are covered in Modules 2 and 3.

1.5 Two SYSINITs#

Both systems call their start-up code "SYSINIT", and the coincidence is a useful teaching device, because the two ideas are almost opposite.

MS-DOS's SYSINIT is a module: code in IO.SYS (SYSINIT1.ASM, SYSCONF.ASM, SYSINIT2.ASM) that runs once, moves itself and the kernel around memory, calls DOSINIT, interprets a text file, and disappears when the shell starts. Its order of work is the order of its instructions; its extensibility comes from CONFIG.SYS, whose lines are reduced to one-letter command codes:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 1.22 – The CONFIG.SYS keyword table: each keyword becomes a one-letter command code (SYSINIT2.ASM lines 1500-1522)Source ↗
COMTAB  LABEL   BYTE
;;;;       DB      8,"AVAILDEV",'A'     ; NO LONGER SUPPORTED
        DB      7,"BUFFERS",  'B'
        DB      5,"BREAK",    'C'
        DB      6,"DEVICE",   'D'
        DB      5,"FILES",    'F'
        DB      4,"FCBS",     'X'
        DB      9,"LASTDRIVE",'L'
        db     10,"MULTITRACK", 'M'     ;AN002;
        DB      8,"DRIVPARM", 'P'       ; RS for DOS 3.2
                IF     STACKSW
        DB      6,"STACKS",   'K'       ; BAS for DOS 3.2
                ENDIF
        DB      7,"COUNTRY",  'Q'
        DB      5,"SHELL",    'S'
        db      7,"INSTALL",  'I'       ;AN000;
        db      3,"IFS",      'J'       ;AN000;
        db      4,"CPSW",     'W'       ;AN000;
;;;;       DB      8,"SWITCHAR",'W'     ; NO LONGER SUPPORTED
        db      7,"COMMENT",  'Y'       ;AN000;
        db      3,"REM",      '0'       ;AN004;
        db      8,"SWITCHES", '1'       ;AN013;
        DB      0

ORGANIZE (SYSINIT2.ASM lines 400-470) upper-cases the file, matches each line's first word against COMTAB with REPE CMPSB, and stores the letter in place of the keyword; unknown keywords become Z ("Unrecognized command in CONFIG.SYS"). DOCONF then dispatches on the letters (TryB for BUFFERS=, TRYDJ for DEVICE= and IFS=, and so on). In 4.00 the file is processed in several passes over the same buffer, selected by Multi_Pass_Id (SYSCONF.ASM lines 797-853): an initial pass that loads XMAEM.SYS and pre-scans BUFFERS= for the /X (expanded memory) option, the main pass for everything else, a pass for IFS= lines, and a last pass that runs the INSTALL= programs. So, for example, every INSTALL= program runs after every DEVICE= driver, whatever their order in the file.

FreeBSD's SYSINIT() is a declaration: a macro that any kernel source file, or any loadable module, uses to say "call this function with this argument at this stage of start-up". No central file lists the stages' contents.

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 1.23 – struct sysinit and the SYSINIT() macro (non-TSLOG variant) (kernel.h lines 226-282)Source ↗
struct sysinit {
        enum sysinit_sub_id     subsystem;      /* subsystem identifier */
        enum sysinit_elem_order order;          /* init order within subsystem */
        STAILQ_ENTRY(sysinit)   next;           /* singly-linked list */
        sysinit_cfunc_t func;                   /* function */
        const void      *udata;                 /* multiplexer/argument */
};
⋮
#define C_SYSINIT(uniquifier, subsystem, order, func, ident)    \
        static struct sysinit uniquifier ## _sys_init = {       \
                subsystem,                                      \
                order,                                          \
                { NULL },                                       \
                func,                                           \
                (ident)                                         \
        };                                                      \
        DATA_WSET(sysinit_set, uniquifier ## _sys_init)
#endif

#define SYSINIT(uniquifier, subsystem, order, func, ident)      \
        C_SYSINIT(uniquifier, subsystem, order,                 \
        (sysinit_cfunc_t)(sysinit_nfunc_t)func, (void *)(ident))

Each use creates a static struct sysinit and adds a pointer to it to the linker set sysinit_set through DATA_WSET. A linker set is FreeBSD's way of building an array out of declarations scattered over many object files:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 1.24 – A linker-set entry is a pointer placed in an ELF section named set_<name> (linker_set.h lines 66-72)Source ↗
#define __MAKE_SET_QV(set, sym, qv)                     \
        __WEAK(__CONCAT(__start_set_,set));             \
        __WEAK(__CONCAT(__stop_set_,set));              \
        static void const * qv                          \
        __NOASAN                                        \
        __set_##set##_sym_##sym __section("set_" #set)  \
        __used = &(sym)

Every pointer goes into the ELF section set_sysinit_set. The linker concatenates same-named sections from all object files and, because the section name is a valid C identifier, defines the symbols __start_set_sysinit_set and __stop_set_sysinit_set around the result. SET_BEGIN and SET_LIMIT (lines 88-95) refer to those symbols, which is how mi_startup() (Listing 1.20) finds all entries without anyone having registered them at run time. sysinit_mklist() copies the pointers into a list and merge-sorts it (lines 190-206) with sysinit_compar(), which orders entries by subsystem and then by order (lines 175-188). The subsystem numbers form a coarse timeline: SI_SUB_TUNABLES (0x0700000), SI_SUB_COPYRIGHT, SI_SUB_VM (0x1000000), SI_SUB_KLD, SI_SUB_INTRINSIC (process 0), SI_SUB_CREATE_INIT (0x2500000), SI_SUB_DRIVERS, SI_SUB_CONFIGURE, SI_SUB_VFS, …, SI_SUB_ROOT_CONF, SI_SUB_KTHREAD_INIT (0xe000000), up to SI_SUB_LAST (enum sysinit_sub_id); SI_ORDER_* values order entries within one subsystem (lines 184-198). The values are explicit numbers with gaps "to provide for binary compatibility with inserted elements": a module compiled today must still sort correctly against a kernel that later adds a stage. Examples from init_main.c itself: process 0 is set up by SYSINIT(p0init, SI_SUB_INTRINSIC, SI_ORDER_FIRST, proc0_init, NULL) (line 649), and the two init steps of Section 1.4 are at line 859 and line 874. Even kernel tunables (values from loader.conf read with TUNABLE_INT) are implemented as SYSINIT entries at SI_SUB_TUNABLES (lines 318-330).

One documentation detail: the SYSINIT(9) manual page for 15.1 still shows the list link as SLIST_ENTRY, while the 15.1 header uses STAILQ_ENTRY and mi_startup() uses STAILQ_MERGESORT. As elsewhere in this course, the source is the reference.

MS-DOS 4.00 SYSINIT FreeBSD 15.1 SYSINIT()
What it is A module of IO.SYS (about 225 KB of assembler source in three files) A macro creating a struct sysinit in a linker set
Who decides the order The programmer, by the order of instructions, plus the fixed passes over CONFIG.SYS Each entry's (subsystem, order) pair; mi_startup() sorts
Configuration input CONFIG.SYS, parsed by SYSINIT itself loader.conf, parsed by the loader and passed as kernel environment
Third-party code joins by DEVICE=, IFS=, INSTALL= lines that name files Being linked into the kernel or loaded as a module with its own SYSINIT entries
Runs Once, in real mode, then its memory is freed Once per entry at boot; modules loaded later run their own entries at load time
Ends with INT 21h EXEC of the shell (Listing 1.16) kern_execve() of /sbin/init in process 1

Study case 1.C looks at the third-party paths in detail.

Study cases#

Study case 1.A: The 512 bytes#

Goal. Account for every byte of two boot sectors, MS-DOS 4.00's FAT boot sector and FreeBSD 15.1's boot0, and relate each region to the source line that produced it.

Guided walk. Start with MSBOOT. The table gives the layout of the sector as assembled from this tree (it is the image that ends up in INC\BOOT.INC; the lab build's BOOT\MSBOOT.BIN holds it at file offset 0x7C00). On a formatted disk, FORMAT will have replaced the BPB values and Phydrv; on the lab image build/images/dos400.img, tools/make_floppy.py did the same (Module 0, Section 0.4).

Offset Size Field (MSBOOT.ASM name) Assembled value
0x000 3 JMP START (+ NOP) EB 3C 90
0x003 8 OEM name MSDOS4.0
0x00B 2 ByteSec, bytes per sector 0x0200
0x00D 1 sectors per cluster 0x08
0x00E 2 cSecRes, reserved sectors 0x0001
0x010 1 cFat, number of FATs 0x02
0x011 2 DirNum, root directory entries 0x0200
0x013 2 cTotSec, total sectors (16-bit) 0x5103 (= 417305-1)
0x015 1 MEDIA, media descriptor 0xF8
0x016 2 cSecFat, sectors per FAT 0x0008
0x018 2 SECLIM, sectors per track 0x0011
0x01A 2 HDLIM, heads 0x0004
0x01C 4 Ext_cSecHid, hidden sectors 0x00000001
0x020 4 Ext_cTotSec, total sectors (32-bit) 0
0x024 1 Phydrv, BIOS drive number 0x80
0x025 1 Curhd, scratch "current head" 0x00
0x026 1 Ext_Boot_Sig 0x29 (decimal 41)
0x027 4 Boot_Serial 0 (set by FORMAT)
0x02B 11 Boot_Vol_Label NO NAME + spaces
0x036 8 Boot_System_id FAT12 + spaces
0x03E 341 code, from START to the end of DOCALL
0x193 72 SYSMSG, CR/LF-framed and NUL-terminated "Non-System disk or disk error…"
0x1DB 22 BIO, DOS file names IO SYS, MSDOS SYS
0x1F1 13 unused (zero)
0x1FE 2 signature 55 AA

The variables BIOS$, CURTRK, CURSEC and DIR$ overlay the first instructions, like the diskette table (UDATA, lines 136-144). The assembler computes the remaining space as Free EQU (cbSec - 4) - ($-$start), 11 bytes, and BOOT.SKL warns translators that the message can grow by at most that much. Space pressure explains the arithmetic routine too:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 1.25 – DODIV converts a 32-bit sector number to sector, head and track (MSBOOT.ASM lines 428-438)Source ↗
DODIV:
        cmp     dx,Seclim               ;AN000; To prevent overflow!!!
        jae     DivOverFlow             ;AN000; Compare high word with the divisor.
        DIV     SECLIM                  ;AX = Total tracks, DX = sector number
        INC     DL                      ;Since we assume SecLim < 255 (a byte), DH =0.
                                        ;Cursec is 1-based.
        MOV     CURSEC, DL              ;save it
        XOR     DX,DX
        DIV     HDLIM
        MOV     CURHD,DL                ;Also, Hdlim < 255.
        MOV     CURTRK,AX

An 8086 DIV divides DX:AX by a 16-bit value and faults if the quotient does not fit in 16 bits. DODIV therefore refuses (carry set) when the high word is not smaller than SECLIM. A full 32-bit division is present in the file, commented out with "We don't have space for the following full 32 bit division" (lines 446-478). The consequence: every sector MSBOOT reads must have a number below SECLIM * 65536. With 17 sectors per track that is 1,114,112 sectors (570,425,344 bytes, about 544 MB); with 63 sectors per track, 4,128,768 sectors (about 2 GB). Also note what is not checked: DOCALL (lines 484-494) shifts DH (cylinder bits 8-15) left by 6, so cylinder bits above bit 9 are silently lost, and a directory beyond cylinder 1023 would be read from the wrong place and fail the name check.

Now boot0. The second table was derived from the lab's build/freebsd/boot/boot0 (512 bytes) with hexdump -C and matched against boot0.S assembled with the default options -DVOLUME_SERIAL -DPXE.

Offset Size Content (boot0.S label) Bytes in the shipped file
0x000 381 code, start to the end of intx13 starts FC 31 C0 8E C0 ...
0x17D 18 prompt ("F6 PXE", "Boot:"), item, crlf 46 36 20 20 50 58 45 0D ...
0x18F 7 bootable_ids 83 A5 A6 A9 06 07 0B
0x196 8 desc_ofs, one-byte relative offsets 0C 10 13 12 05 04 03 01
0x19E 16 os_misc, os_win, os_linux, os_freebsd/os_bsd BF 57 69 EE 4C ...
0x1AE 6 drive: Drive 44 72 69 76 65 20
0x1B4 4 nxtdrv, opt (default: F1), setdrv_num, flags 00 00 80 8F
0x1B8 4 volume serial (Windows disk signature) A8 A8 A8 A8
0x1BC 2 ticks B6 00 (182 ticks, about 10 s)
0x1BE 64 partbl, the partition table zeros in the file
0x1FE 2 MAGIC 55 AA

In the source (boot0.S lines 647-673), .org (0x200 + B0_OFF),0x90 pads with NOPs up to the parameter block, and the final .org 0x200 is a "safety check": if the code grew too large, assembly fails instead of silently moving the table. MSBOOT only warns: if Free LT 0 prints "FATAL PROBLEM: boot sector is too large" with %out, and the build goes on (lines 508-526). Note the high-bit string terminator ('n'|0x80 is EE) and the shared bytes: os_freebsd is Free followed directly by os_bsd's BSD.

What to notice.

  • Both sectors keep their configuration inside the sector at fixed offsets that external tools depend on: FORMAT and SYS write MSBOOT's BPB and Phydrv; boot0cfg edits opt, flags, ticks and the serial. Both sources contain comments warning that these offsets must not move (MSBOOT lines 517-524, boot0.S lines 648-655).
  • MSBOOT spends its bytes on file-system knowledge (BPB arithmetic, directory names); boot0 knows nothing about any file system and spends its bytes on a user interface.
  • Both check the 512-byte limit at assembly time, but only boot0's build fails on overflow; MSBOOT's assembly prints a warning.
MSBOOT (FAT VBR) boot0 (MBR)
Code bytes 341 381
Data the OS cares about BPB (0x00B-0x03D) partition table (0x1BE-0x1FD)
Configuration bytes BPB, Phydrv (written by FORMAT/SYS) 0x1B4-0x1BD (written by boot0cfg and by boot0 itself)
Disk interface CHS, DODIV limited by SECLIM * 65536 EDD packets or CHS
Space-saving tricks variables over executed code; 16-bit-only division BP-relative variables; high-bit string ends; carry-terminated loop
Free bytes 11 by Free, 13 zero bytes none spare: DOS label dropped to fit PXE

Discussion questions.

  1. MSBOOT trusts the BPB in its own sector; boot1 re-reads the MBR to find its slice. What happens to each when a partition is moved to a different starting sector with a disk-copy tool?
  2. If you had to add one feature to MSBOOT, for example a retry loop on read errors, which existing bytes would you sacrifice, and which constraint from Section 1.3 might become stricter?
  3. The shipped boot0 labels a FAT16 partition "Win" because "DOS" did not fit next to the PXE entry. Is that an acceptable trade-off for a boot manager? Who is affected?

Study case 1.B: Boot code that writes to the disk#

Goal. Understand why boot0 writes its own sector back to disk during every interactive boot, why MS-DOS boot code never writes, and how gptboot performs a safer kind of boot-time write.

Guided walk. After a valid key press, boot0 records the choice and then rewrites sector 0:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 1.26 – boot0 saves the selected option and writes its whole sector back (boot0.S lines 428-463)Source ↗
                movb %al,_OPT(%bp)              # Save option
⋮
                movw %bp,%si                    # Partition for write
                movb (%si),%dl                  # Drive number, saved above
                movw %si,%bx                    # Partition for read
                cmpb $0x4,%al                   # F5/#5 pressed?
                pushf                           # Save results for later
                je 1f                           # Yes, F5

        /*
         * F1..F4 was pressed, so make %bx point to the currently
         * selected partition, and leave the drive number unchanged.
         */
                shlb $0x4,%al                   # Point to
                addw $partbl,%ax                #  selected
                xchgw %bx,%ax                   #  partition
                movb $0x80,(%bx)                # Flag active
        /*
         * If not asked to do a write-back (flags 0x40) don't do one.
         * Around the call, save the partition pointer to %bx and
         * restore to %si which is where the next stage expects it.
         */
        1:      pushw %bx                       # Save
                testb $NOUPDATE,_FLAGS(%bp)     # No updates?
                jnz 2f                          # skip update
                movw $start,%bx                 # Data to write
                movb $0x3,%ah                   # Write sector
                callw intx13                    #  to disk
        2:      popw %si                        # Restore

_OPT(%bp) is the opt byte at 0x1B5 of the in-memory copy. The selected entry gets 0x80; the menu loop had already cleared every active flag (Listing 1.6), so exactly one entry is active, the invariant FDBOOT checks. intx13 with AH=3 and the fake entry at BP (LBA 0) writes the 512 bytes at 0x600, code, options and modified table, to sector 0; in packet mode it turns AX=0301h into 4300h, the EDD write with "verify off" (lines 552-576). Four details matter:

  1. It happens only after an explicit key press: on timeout or Enter, use_default sets NOUPDATE first (lines 366-368); a forced drive (setdrv) also disables updates.
  2. It happens before the chosen boot sector is read and checked, so an unbootable choice still becomes the default and the active partition.
  3. Its return status is ignored (2: popw %si follows the call), so write-protected media still boot.
  4. boot0cfg -o noupdate sets flag 0x40 permanently; the default flags value 0x8f does not (Makefile lines 19-30).

gptboot also writes during boot, but differently. For a partition marked bootonce, it clears bootme in both the primary and the backup GPT before booting, so that a failed test boot falls back to the old system next time:
